title: A weekly sit with others
hookLine: a sangha night, in person or online
tomorrow: Sunday off. Jess wants the museum; Mai wants quiet. can it be both?

lines: A THURSDAY SIT FULL OF STRANGERS.
cards: Mai found a Thursday night sit at a Vietnamese temple near the program: a bus ride away, every face a stranger. Why go, when she could sit alone in her room? The suttas hide an answer inside a war story.
A king wants to attack a neighboring people, the Vajjians, and sends his chief minister to ask the Buddha how it will go. The Buddha doesn't answer the minister.
He turns to Ananda and asks: have you heard that the Vajjians meet often, and in full numbers? Why would a question about war get an answer about meetings?

teach.b: Because to the Buddha, that was the answer. As long as the Vajjians kept meeting often, and met and parted in harmony, he said, they could be expected to prosper and not decline.
It's the first condition on his list, and the minister leaves concluding the king can't beat them by force alone.

teach.h: THE SAME LIST FOR THE MONKS.
teach.b: Then, in the same sutta, the Buddha gathers the monks and gives them a list for the sangha.
First on it, again: as long as you meet together often and in full numbers, expect to grow, not decline. That's the puzzle solved. Meeting isn't a social extra.
In the Buddha's own order, it's where a community's health begins. A practice kept only alone has nobody to notice when it drifts.

teach.h: A ROOM THAT HOLDS YOU THERE.
teach.b: A room of people sitting in silence holds you there on the nights your own effort wouldn't. It's the root of the weekly sangha night you'll find at temples, at meditation centers, in living rooms and on video calls.
And listen to the word in the sutta: often. Not once, when you're in the mood.
Every week. Strangers don't stay strangers long when you sit beside them every Thursday.

how: Buddhist temples, meditation centers and small sanghas hold weekly sitting nights, in person and online: a period of sitting, sometimes walking meditation or chanting, and often a short talk or discussion.

games.q: what does “a weekly sit with others” mean?
o: sitting alone at home while a group meets online
sitting with a community, regularly, every week
a yearly gathering for a big Buddhist festival

games.q: the war story's answer — tap the pairs.
p: were given the same first condition

s: the Buddha told the king's minister how to win the war
he answered with how the Vajjians stay strong: meeting often, in harmony.
in the same sutta, meeting often is first on the Buddha's list for the monks too
as long as they meet together often and in full numbers, they can be expected to grow.
Buddhist practice is meant to be done alone; groups are optional
the Buddha puts meeting together first among the conditions for a community that lasts.

games.q: your temple's weekly sit has shrunk to four regulars. one asks, 'why keep it going for so few?' what fits today's teaching?
o: keep meeting every week; meeting often is the first condition for lasting
pause it until enough people sign up to make it worthwhile
meet only on big festival days, when the crowds come
games.why: the Buddha's first condition is meeting often, not meeting big. a small room that meets every week keeps a community alive.

practice: Listen for one steady sound around you, a fan, traffic, a voice in another room, and let it stand for everyone else sitting somewhere right now. Breathe with it for the two minutes. You're sitting alone, and also not.

wordCard.voice: A weekly sit with others: meeting often, in harmony, the first condition the Buddha named for a community that lasts.

orig.note: Pali: an assembly, a community. The Buddhist community, and the third of the three refuges.

carryVoice: Keep this: every week, because the Buddha put meeting often first on his list. Thursday's coming.

sources.ref: Digha Nikaya 16 (Mahaparinibbana Sutta), I.1–6: the Vajjians' conditions of welfare and the same conditions for the monks
